areas.n: East Side (Hyde Park, Oakley, Mt. Lookout)

P.n: Cincinnati Museum Center at Union Terminal
P.w: One of the last grand Art Deco railroad terminals (1933), a National Historic Landmark whose half-dome rotunda now houses the History, Natural History & Science, and Children's museums plus an OMNIMAX theater.
P.k: Multi-museum complex; check which museums/exhibits are open before visiting.

P.ad: 100 W Mehring Way, Cincinnati, OH 45202 (Covington side: 200 Riverside Dr, Covington, KY 41011)
P.w: Opened 1867 as the longest suspension span in the world, John A. Roebling's Ohio River bridge was the prototype for his Brooklyn Bridge; its illuminated cables are Cincinnati's signature riverfront image.

P.n: Fountain Square & the Tyler Davidson Fountain
P.w: The city's civic living room since 1871, anchored by 'The Genius of Water,' Ferdinand von Miller's bronze fountain gifted by Henry Probasco in memory of Tyler Davidson.
The 49th-floor open-air deck atop the 1931 Art Deco Carew Tower (by the Empire State Building's architects) long gave the best downtown-and-river panorama.
P.k: Deck closed as of 2026 during the tower's conversion to apartments; slated to reopen but no date announced. The building's ground-floor Art Deco arcade remains accessible.

P.w: Samuel Hannaford's 1878 High Victorian Gothic landmark facing Washington Park, home to the Cincinnati Symphony, Pops, Opera and Ballet, reopened in 2017 after a $143M restoration.
Opened 2004 on the riverfront where escaping slaves crossed the Ohio, this museum tells the story of the Underground Railroad and contemporary freedom struggles, anchored by a rescued slave pen.
The nation's second-oldest zoo (1875) and an accredited botanical garden, now world-famous as the home of Fiona the hippo, born prematurely in 2017.
Ohio's oldest continuously operated public market (1855), an iron-framed OTR institution packed with Eckerlin Meats, Pho Lang Thang and dozens of vendors plus a weekend farmers' market.
A restored 6-acre park (reopened 2012) across from Music Hall with an interactive fountain, bandstand and event lawn, the green heart of Over-the-Rhine's revival.

P.n: Great American Ball Park & Reds Hall of Fame
P.w: Riverfront home of the Cincinnati Reds, baseball's oldest professional franchise, since 2003; the adjoining Reds Hall of Fame & Museum honors the Big Red Machine.
The riverfront home of the NFL's Cincinnati Bengals since 2000 (formerly Paul Brown Stadium), part of the downtown sports-and-Banks corridor.
FC Cincinnati's $250M soccer-specific stadium in the West End, opened 2021, known for a translucent LED-lit facade and one of MLS's loudest atmospheres.

P.n: Smale Riverfront Park & Carol Ann's Carousel
P.w: A landscaped riverfront park between the ballpark and stadium with swings, water features and Carol Ann's Carousel, whose 44 hand-carved animals honor Cincinnati history.

P.ad: 705 E Pete Rose Way, Cincinnati, OH 45202
P.w: A mile of riverfront park at Yeatman's Cove where the stepped Serpentine Wall (1976) descends to the Ohio, a classic spot to sit and watch the river and the Kentucky skyline.
A 2,670-ft former rail bridge, restored in 2006 as a purple-painted pedestrian-only crossing linking Newport on the Levee to downtown Cincinnati with skyline views.
A riverfront aquarium at Newport on the Levee with 20,000+ animals, walk-through acrylic tunnels and a rope 'Shark Bridge' suspended over the sharks.

P.ad: Main St & W 6th St, Covington, KY 41011
P.w: A restored 19th-century German neighborhood in Covington with Italianate storefronts, bars and the Carroll Chimes Bell Tower's animated Pied Piper show over the Goose Girl Fountain.
The Drees Pavilion overlook in Covington's 700-acre Devou Park frames the definitive postcard view of the Cincinnati skyline across the Ohio, renovated in 2024.

P.ad: Vine St & E 12th St, Cincinnati, OH 45202
P.w: One of the largest, most intact urban historic districts in the U.S. (NRHP 1983, ~943 contributing buildings) with the country's largest contiguous collection of 19th-century Italianate architecture, built by German immigrants.
Long-running Ohio River sightseeing, lunch and dinner cruises departing the Newport landing on Riverboat Row, across from downtown Cincinnati.
P.k: Regular sightseeing schedule runs roughly Memorial Day to Labor Day; check dates.

P.w: A multi-level riverfront dining and entertainment complex (opened 2001) housing the Newport Aquarium, a food hall, cinema and comedy club, at the foot of the Purple People Bridge.
An 18-acre mixed-use riverfront district tucked between the ballpark and Paycor Stadium, tying together restaurants, bars and residences alongside Smale Park and the Freedom Center.
Encyclopedic collection of 67,000+ works spanning 6,000 years, perched in Eden Park; general admission and parking are always free.
P.k: Free general admission; closed Mondays (Tue–Sun 11–5, Thu to 8).

P.w: European old masters (Rembrandt, Turner, Hals, Ingres) plus Chinese porcelains and French Renaissance enamels inside an 1820 Federal mansion with Robert S. Duncanson murals; bequeathed to the city in 1927.
P.k: Historic house museum, small but exceptional; check hours.

P.w: Zaha Hadid's 2003 Lois & Richard Rosenthal Center — the first American art museum designed by a woman, an internationally studied piece of architecture at 6th & Walnut.
P.k: Rotating contemporary shows; the building itself is the draw.

P.w: The nation's largest public sign museum — a glowing indoor streetscape of vintage neon and Americana signage in Camp Washington.
P.k: Closed Mon–Tue (Wed–Sun 10–4).

P.w: 200+ years of firefighting history in the restored 1906 Court Street Firehouse — Cincinnati created the nation's first paid professional fire department in 1853.
P.k: Housed in a National Register 1906 firehouse; limited hours.

P.w: Ohio's oldest brick house (1804) and the anchor of the Betts-Longworth Historic District — now a small museum of the built environment in the West End.
P.k: Very small; check for open days/guided tours.

P.w: Northern Kentucky's regional history and natural history museum, set inside Devou Park with skyline views over the river.
P.k: In Devou Park (NKY); closed Mondays.

P.w: Cincinnati's grand hilltop park above the river — the Twin Lakes overlook gives one of the best Ohio River views in the city, plus the Presidential Grove of memorial oaks (first planted 1882 for Washington).
P.k: Free, open daily; overlook is in the NE corner.

P.w: Art Deco glasshouse in Eden Park (1933) with rainforest, desert and orchid houses and a beloved annual spring butterfly show.
P.k: Small admission for special shows; closed Mondays.

P.w: 224-acre Mt. Lookout park crowned by a 1930 Italian Renaissance pavilion; climb to the overlook for panoramic views across the Little Miami valley.
P.k: Free; hilltop pavilion is a popular event venue.

P.w: At 1,459 acres Cincinnati's largest park and one of the country's largest urban forests, with miles of trails and a free 120-acre arboretum.
P.k: Free; huge — pick a trailhead or the arboretum.

P.w: A National Historic Landmark garden cemetery (1844) — 733 acres of lakes, monuments and champion trees, one of the largest cemeteries in the US and a designated arboretum.
P.k: Free; a working cemetery — be respectful.

P.w: 1,000+ acres of woodland trails, ponds and a nature center in Milford — a longtime regional favorite for hiking and birding.
P.k: Admission/membership; east-suburb drive.

P.w: Hilltop Mt. Lookout park on Mt. Tusculum with several overlooks taking in the Ohio and Little Miami rivers, the NKY hills and Lunken Airport.
P.k: Free, open daily 6a–10p.

P.w: The oldest professional observatory in the US and 'Birthplace of American Astronomy,' with one of the world's oldest working telescopes; on its Mt. Lookout hilltop since 1873.
P.k: Public viewing nights and tours — check schedule.

P.w: Hillside artists' neighborhood of steep streets and skyline views; its 1859 Immaculata Church draws 10,000+ pilgrims each Good Friday to 'Pray the Steps' up St. Gregory St.
P.k: Church is active; the Good Friday steps tradition is the signature draw.

P.w: Clifton Heights hillside park with a grand, wide-open view over the entire Cincinnati basin, downtown skyline and the Ohio River.
P.k: Free; small neighborhood park (not the NKY Bellevue).

P.w: One of the best-preserved Moorish Revival buildings in the US (1866), a National Historic Landmark tied to Reform Judaism founder Rabbi Isaac Mayer Wise.
P.k: Active synagogue; interior by tour/arrangement.

P.n: Cathedral Basilica of St. Peter in Chains
P.w: Greek Revival 'White Angel' cathedral (1845) at 8th & Plum with a soaring spire and mosaic interior, seat of the Archdiocese of Cincinnati.
P.k: Active cathedral; open for visits around services.

P.n: William Howard Taft National Historic Site
P.w: NPS-run birthplace and boyhood home of the only man to serve as both US President and Chief Justice, in the Mt. Auburn Historic District.
P.k: Free NPS site; ranger tours of the restored home.

P.w: Walnut Hills home where the future 'Uncle Tom's Cabin' author lived; now an Ohio History Connection museum on abolition and Cincinnati's Black history, reopened after a $2.5M renovation.
P.k: Limited hours; recently renovated.

P.w: A medieval-style stone castle on the Little Miami River hand-built over decades starting 1927 by WWI vet and Boy Scout leader Harry Andrews — a beloved regional oddity.
P.k: Seasonal/weekend hours; NE-suburb drive to Loveland.

P.w: The 1892 Tudor-style Mt. Adams pottery works of famed Rookwood Pottery, its old kilns big enough to dine in; now a restaurant/bar with skyline views.
P.k: Building now a restaurant — exterior/architecture and kiln dining rooms are the draw.

P.w: Cincinnati's most charming shopping square, centered on the classical 1900 Kilgour Fountain and a grassy green, lined with 100+ boutiques and cafes.
P.k: Walkable district; Sunday farmers' market mid-May–Oct.

P.w: A National Historic Landmark 'garden city' — one of America's first fully planned suburbs, laid out in the 1920s by Mary Emery and John Nolen in Tudor-village style with a central concourse and carillon.
P.k: Historic village ~10 mi east; stroll the square.

P.ad: Hamilton Ave & Hoffner St, Cincinnati, OH 45223
P.w: Cincinnati's most eclectic, creative neighborhood — a two-mile stretch of Hamilton Ave lined with locally-owned restaurants, vintage shops, record stores and music venues amid the Italianate Hoffner Historic District.
P.k: Best explored on foot; nightlife-heavy.

P.w: Regional icon 24 miles NE in Mason — a 364-acre amusement park with 15+ coasters, an Eiffel Tower replica and the Soak City water park, open since 1972.
P.k: Seasonal (spring–fall + Halloween/holiday events); paid admission.

P.w: Once home to the world's largest indoor model-train display (25,000 sq ft, 2+ miles of track) in West Chester.
P.k: CLOSED — permanently shut January 5, 2025. Listed for reference; do not visit.

F.w: Cincinnati's only James Beard honoree for chili (America's Classic, 2000) — a 24-hour parlor since 1940. Order the 5-way: spaghetti, cinnamon-clove chili, kidney beans, diced onion and a mountain of shredded cheddar; the cheese coneys are the sleeper order.

The defining Cincinnati-chili brand, founded 1949 by Greek immigrant Nicholas Lambrinides. The downtown parlor is the classic city stop for a cheese coney (mustard, chili, mound of cheddar) and the 4-way onion.
s: 10Best readers' polls repeatedly rank Skyline atop Cincinnati chili — see USA Today 10Best Cincinnati chili

F.w: A neighborhood parlor run by three generations of the Sideris family since 1964, beloved as much for its award-winning gravy cheese fries as its 2-through-5-way chili and homemade coneys.

Skyline's cross-town rival, born 1965 in Mt. Washington as 'Hamburger Heaven' before the Daoud brothers' chili took over the menu. The original location is the spot for a Gold Star cheese coney and 4-way.
s: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Star_Chili — founded 1965, Mt. Washington, Daoud brothers

F.w: A 1969 Blue Ash institution twice featured on Guy Fieri's 'Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives' — he called the 5-way something he'd eat every day. Add jalapenos for the house 6-way.
s: wcpo.com/best-cincinnati-chili-restaurants — Top chili parlors in the Tri-State

F.w: A West Side family restaurant since 1962 with the Golden Fleece Lounge attached — Cincinnati chili 2-through-5-way, cheese coneys, Greek favorites and big all-day breakfasts.
Northern Kentucky's first chili parlor, founded 1929 by Nicholas Sarakatsannis and still slinging 3-, 4- and 5-ways and coneys into the small hours across the river in Newport.
A sassy pink diner (since 1941) famous for 'wispy thin' pancakes and crisp-griddled goetta — the German pork-and-oats loaf that is Cincinnati's own breakfast meat.
s: Cincinnati breakfast institution — wcpo.com coverage; also Roadfood.com

F.w: An old-fashioned Findlay Market butcher, family-run since 1852, voted Cincinnati's Best Goetta and selling 400-500 lbs a week — the goetta many city diners (including Tucker's) buy to griddle. Grab a loaf plus the house mettwurst.
s: Twice voted 'Best Goetta' by Cincinnati Magazine — cincinnatifoodtours.com/blog/cincinnati-goetta; local12.com Eckerlin coverage

F.w: Cincinnati's 'Ribs King' since 1951 — Ted Gregory's slow-cooked ribs lacquered in Matula Gregory's sweet tangy sauce. The original Montgomery Road room is the mothership (a downtown Boathouse followed in 1989).
A riverside East End smoke shack that turned into a Cincinnati favorite: hickory pulled pork, ribs, all-beef dogs and the cult jalapeno-cheddar grits. Cash-friendly, picnic-table casual.
s: Frequent Cincinnati Magazine BBQ pick; cincinnatibites.com/reviews/elis-bbq/
Repeatedly cited among the city's best BBQ — citybeat.com food coverage

F.w: Cincinnati's standout Vietnamese kitchen, grown from a Findlay Market stall (2011) to a full Race Street room with a bar. 20-hour broth from Ohio Sakura Farms Wagyu, lemongrass grilled pork, sharp banh mi.
Began 2007 as a 120-lb cast-iron waffle iron in the back of a Findlay Market produce shop; now the caramelized-sugar Liege waffle and the waffle-and-fried-chicken are a Cincinnati brunch signature.
s: Cincinnati Magazine dining coverage of Taste of Belgium's Findlay Market origin

F.w: French-pot ice cream, hand-packed 2.5-gallon batches since 1870, with giant chocolate chunks. Cincinnati Magazine named the black raspberry chip a flavor that 'defines' the city; the Hyde Park scoop shop is the classic stop.
s: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeter's — Cincinnati Magazine named black raspberry chip a defining city food (2004)
Cincinnati Magazine — black raspberry chip among foods that define Cincinnati

F.w: An Oakley Square parlor barely changed since 1913 — Portuguese marble, Tiffany lamps, hand-laid tile — where the Greek Aglamesis family still makes French-pot ice cream and hand-dipped chocolates.

O'Bryonville patisserie (since 1983) whose signature is the Opera Cream Torte — dark chocolate, white chocolate and vanilla opera cream, a distinctly Cincinnati confection — plus schnecken and whimsical iced cookies.
A hometown tradition since 1928, best known for the yellow-iced 'smiley' cookie (a Cincinnati billboard icon) and buttery schnecken. The Hyde Park shop is the flagship counter.
Family-run since 1960 and repeatedly called Cincinnati's gold-standard doughnut — hand-cut, hand-dipped, from glazed to maple-bacon. Loveland is the original shop (the OTR location has since closed).
s: USA Today 10Best Readers' Choice — Holtman's ranked among best U.S. doughnut shops

F.w: A Covington Westside beer hall built on scratch-ground German sausages — Feuerwurst, currywurst, apple-honey wurst — with schnitzel, giant pretzels with beer cheese and 40+ German/craft taps.
The Cincinnati pizza icon: Buddy LaRosa opened here in 1954 using his Aunt Dena's Sicilian recipe (sweeter provolone-topped pies). The original Westwood parlor is the fan-favorite original.

Wood-fired pies from a restored 150-year-old Walnut Hills firehouse (Engine Co. #16) — a rotating menu of blistered-crust specialty pizzas backed by a deep local beer list. The city's best neighborhood wood-fired option.
David Falk's flagship in the old Maisonette space — award-winning European cooking with French precision; Cincinnati Magazine's No. 1 Best Restaurant.
Candlelit subterranean Italian below Boca — famed short rib cappellacci and truffle-season tajarin; Cincinnati Magazine No. 3 Best Restaurant.
Jose Salazar's namesake restaurant, reopened Nov 2025 in the former Saks/Paycor building. Salazar is a 2024 James Beard finalist for Best Chef: Great Lakes.
Chef Jose Salazar's Spanish/Latin American tapas room named for his Colombian grandmother; Salazar is a James Beard nominee/finalist.
David Falk's upscale modern-Mexican room on the Aronoff plaza — reimagined menu and one of downtown's best patios (confirmed open 2025).
Thunderdome Group's homage to founders' Italian grandparents — pasta made fresh daily; voted Best Italian by CityBeat readers 2025 and a 2026 Yelp Top-100 pick.
OTR walk-up window (in the old Lucy Blue pizza slot) famed for the Turtle Shell and house salsas; a late-night and lunch institution.
Longtime Cincinnati Thai favorite reopened across from Washington Park; voted CityBeat's Best Thai 2025.
The brewery that helped launch OTR's beer revival, in the 1890s Christian Moerlein bottling hall; flagship Truth IPA and a rooftop bar. CityBeat's Best Local Brewery.
Oakley powerhouse with a 20+ tap taproom, wood-fired pizza and beer garden; repeatedly voted among Cincinnati's best breweries.
Madisonville taqueria steeped in Oaxacan cooking — widely called Cincinnati's best Mexican; from-scratch salsas and moles.
Mt. Lookout neighborhood tavern, a near-century old; a perennial CityBeat Best Burger and named Ohio's best burger by Food & Wine.
No-frills Norwood grill serving the same cheeseburger since 1966 — the purest expression of the local tavern burger and a repeat Best Cheeseburger winner.
Neon-drenched East End icon (ex-Terry's Turf Club, on Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives) reopened under new local owners Jan 2025, still building maximalist burgers.
Chef Hideki Harada's izakaya and sushi bar in Clifton's Gaslight district; Harada is a 2023 and 2026 James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef: Great Lakes.
Black-owned Texas-style barbecue that consolidated to its College Hill flagship in 2026; brisket smoked low-and-slow, praised mac and cornbread.
Covington brewery that anchored 7th Street's revival — flagship Storm cream ale and one of NKY's only rooftop taprooms overlooking the river skyline.
Stephen Williams's pioneering NKY farm-to-table bistro sourcing 50+ local farms; Cincinnati Magazine Best Restaurants (No. 9) with a 130-bottle bourbon list.
Dave Willocks's tasting-menu-only Newport flagship — Greater Cincinnati's rarest fine-dining format; Willocks is a 2026 James Beard finalist for Best Chef: Southeast.
Newport roaster and cafe with a barista 'chef's table' Analog Bar; ranked Kentucky's best independent coffee shop, profits funding coffee-origin philanthropy.
